**Video:** [Lec 35 — Stochastic Gradient Descent as a Regularizer](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vKTxP9FsR90)

## Learning goals

- See **input perturbation** as implicit regularization.
- Define **SGD** / minibatch gradients as noisy estimates of $\nabla\widehat{R}$.
- Summarize the ERM+regularization worldview before SVMs.

## Before this clicks

Full-batch GD: $\theta\leftarrow\theta-\alpha\nabla_\theta\widehat{R}(\theta)$ using **all** $n$ points. Regularization so far: penalties, early stopping, architecture. Today: randomness in **data** or **gradients** as another regularizer.

---

## Main ideas

### 1. Perturb the inputs, keep the labels

From $\mathcal{D}=\{(x_i,y_i)\}$, build

$$
\tilde{x}_i=x_i+\varepsilon_i,\qquad\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\alpha^{2}I),
$$

and run ERM on $\tilde{\mathcal{D}}=\{(\tilde{x}_i,y_i)\}$.

Claim (homework-style): ERM on $\tilde{\mathcal{D}}$ $\Leftrightarrow$ **regularized** ERM on $\mathcal{D}$, with strength tied to $\alpha$ (noise scale $\leftrightarrow$ $\lambda$). Intuition: you force the hypothesis to stay stable under small input wiggles — a smoothness / robustness bias.

Same moral appears in modern generative modeling (noise as regularization; vanishing gradients / mode collapse mentioned as forward pointers).

### 2. Stochastic gradient descent

Instead of $\nabla\widehat{R}$ on all data, sample a minibatch $B$ of size $b$ (32, 64, …) and use

$$
\theta\leftarrow\theta-\alpha\,\nabla_\theta\widehat{R}_{B}(\theta),
$$

where $\widehat{R}_{B}$ is the empirical risk on $B$ only. That gradient is a **noisy / stochastic** estimate of the full gradient.

Reasons:

1. **Compute:** full gradients may be infeasible at huge $n$.
2. **Regularization:** empirically, SGD often **generalizes better** than full-batch GD — noise acts like a regularizer (related to not sitting in sharp minima; class emphasis is the regularization effect).

### 3. Course checkpoint

ML algorithms = choose hypothesis class + loss + regularizer, then optimize (usually SGD). Same skeleton for discriminative / generative, supervised / unsupervised.

**Coming next:** kernel methods and **SVMs** (elegant, historically SOTA, less dominant than nets today). Brush up **primal/dual**, Lagrange multipliers, **KKT** conditions. After SVMs: neural nets, backprop, CNN/RNN/Transformers, then trees / unsupervised topics.

---

## Worked mini-example

Squared loss, one parameter, two points. Full gradient averages both. Minibatch size $1$ randomly picks one point’s gradient each step — updates jitter around the full-batch path. That jitter is the “stochastic” in SGD; shrinking the learning rate averages noise over time.

---

## Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|---------------|
| SGD is only for speed | Speed matters, but noise also **regularizes**. |
| Batch size must be 1 | Any $b\ll n$ is stochastic; $b=n$ recovers batch GD. |
| Input noise changes $P_{X,Y}$ | Yes — that distributional change is exactly why the effective objective gains a regularizer. |
